scary.notes: A walkthrough house followed by a meeting with Mickey Mouse in a small room. Nothing frightening, though shy children sometimes balk at the actual meeting.

accessibility.notes: The house and meeting room are level and fully accessible. Interior rooms are narrow, so a large ECV may need to take the alternate route a cast member can point out.

attractions.summary: Walk through Mickey's house and the movie barn, then meet Mickey Mouse himself at the end. The queue is the house.
description: Mickey's House is a walkthrough that doubles as a queue. You move through a furnished cottage — living room, kitchen, laundry, a garden — and then a barn set up as a film studio, before reaching a small room where you meet Mickey Mouse and a photographer takes pictures.

The house is genuinely well dressed and full of small jokes: things on shelves, a radio playing, a workshop with props from old cartoons. Because the queue is the attraction, the wait here feels shorter than the same number of minutes standing in a switchback outside.

This is the most reliable Mickey meeting at Disneyland — he is here throughout operating hours rather than appearing on a schedule — which makes it the right choice if a specific character photograph is the point of your day.
tips: The queue is the walkthrough, so the wait passes quickly. A posted 30 minutes here is far less painful than 30 minutes anywhere else.
Mickey is available all day here, unlike character appearances elsewhere that run on a schedule.
Slow down in the movie barn. It has the most detail in the house and everyone rushes it because they can see the meeting room ahead.
Bring your own camera as well — PhotoPass shoots the meeting, but the photographer will also take pictures on your phone if you ask.
attractions.bestTime: First hour after Toontown opens, or the last hour before it closes.
attractions.typicalWait: 25 to 50 minutes, though the walkthrough format makes it feel shorter.

attractions.name: Minnie's House

scary.notes: A bright, furnished cottage you walk through at your own pace. There is nothing frightening in it.

accessibility.notes: Level throughout and accessible, though the interior rooms are narrow and get congested when Toontown is busy.

attractions.summary: A walkthrough cottage full of things kids can press, open, and set off — the most hands-on interior in the park.
description: Minnie's House is a self-guided walkthrough of a furnished cottage next door to Mickey's. It is smaller and more interactive: a kitchen where the dishwasher runs and a cake rises in the oven when you press a button, a dressing room, an answering machine with messages you can play, and a wishing well outside that talks back.

It takes five to ten minutes and there is no character meeting at the end, which is why the line is dramatically shorter than the one next door. For a four-year-old, the density of things to press here is higher than anywhere else at Disneyland.
It is also air conditioned, uncrowded most of the day, and free of any queue structure. Treat it as a rest stop that happens to entertain a preschooler.
tips: Push everything. Almost every appliance and object in the kitchen and dressing room does something, and most guests walk through without touching anything.
The wishing well in the garden outside responds when you talk to it. Kids find this before adults do.
It is far less crowded than Mickey's House next door because there is no character at the end, which makes it a better use of a busy afternoon.
If the rooms are congested, wait two minutes outside — the interior clears in waves as groups exit.
attractions.bestTime: Mid-afternoon, when it doubles as an air-conditioned break.
attractions.typicalWait: Usually under 10 minutes; often a walk-in.

attractions.name: CenTOONial Park

scary.notes: An open green with a fountain and a climbable tree sculpture. There is nothing frightening about it.

accessibility.notes: Wide level paths, a genuine lawn you can sit on, and interactive elements reachable from a seated position. It is the most accessible unstructured space in Disneyland Park.

attractions.summary: The green at the entrance to Toontown with an interactive fountain and a climbable tree — Disneyland's only real lawn.
description: CenTOONial Park opened in 2023 at the entrance to the rebuilt Toontown. It is a park in the ordinary sense: a lawn you are allowed to sit on, a fountain with interactive water elements that respond to being touched, and a large sculpted tree with hollows and roots that children climb.

Disneyland has almost no unstructured green space, which makes this genuinely unusual. Families use it as a base camp — one adult on the grass with the bags while the others take a child to Runaway Railway or the play yards.
The fountain gets kids lightly wet rather than soaked, which is a different proposition from Donald's Duck Pond nearby. It is the right choice when you want cooling off without a change of clothes.
tips: This is the only lawn in the park you are welcome to sit on. Use it as a regroup point rather than standing in a walkway.
The fountain dampens rather than soaks. If you want a full soaking, that is Donald's Duck Pond thirty seconds away.
Shade is limited on the lawn itself. The tree sculpture and the perimeter have the better shaded spots.
It sits right at the Toontown entrance, so it is the natural meeting point if your party splits up between the rides.
attractions.bestTime: Late afternoon, when the shade improves and the Toontown crowd thins.
attractions.typicalWait: None. Open space, walk in.

attractions.name: Space Mountain
attractions.heightNote: One adult may supervise only one child under 7 on this attraction.

scary.notes: Total darkness is the whole point. There is no big drop and no inversion, but you cannot see the track, which means every turn and dip arrives without warning. Children who ride Big Thunder happily are often undone by this. Adults who are fine on coasters but dislike the dark should take it seriously too.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into a rocket with a lap bar and a reclined seating position that is awkward to get out of. Guests with back or neck problems should avoid it — the turns are sharp and unsignalled. The queue includes a long ramp descent and ascent.

attractions.summary: An indoor coaster in the dark with onboard music and two-across seating. 40 inches, and one adult per child under 7.
description: Space Mountain opened at Disneyland in 1977, five years after the Florida version, and the two are different rides in almost every respect that matters. Disneyland's has a single track rather than two, seats riders two abreast rather than single file, runs a smoother and faster-feeling layout, and pipes a synchronized score through speakers in each rocket.

The trick is not speed — the top speed is modest by modern standards. The trick is that the building is dark enough that your eyes never adjust, so you cannot see the next turn coming. Three minutes of unsignalled banking and dropping produces a much stronger reaction than the physics alone would justify.

The supervision rule matters for families: one adult may accompany only one child under seven. A parent alone with two young riders cannot take both, so plan on rider switch or a second adult. The height requirement is 40 inches, matching Big Thunder and Tiana's, which means a child who clears one clears all three.
experience: The queue descends a long ramp through a corridor of blue light and sound before reaching the load platform, where rockets arrive continuously. You sit reclined with your legs forward, a lap bar comes down, and the onboard audio starts as the rocket leaves.

The launch runs through a tunnel of moving light effects and up a lift, then releases into the dark. From there it is three minutes of banked turns, short dips, and sudden direction changes with nothing but projected stars and the occasional strobe for reference. The music tracks the layout, which makes the drops land harder because you can hear them coming without seeing them.

The back rows are the fastest and roughest, as with any coaster. The front gives you the clearest view of the light effects and a slightly gentler ride. Either way you finish on a long, bright braking run and a walk out past the on-ride photo.
tips: Ride it first thing or during the fireworks. It closes for the show if the pyrotechnic safety zone requires it, and reopens with a very short line.
One adult may supervise only one child under seven. This catches out single parents with two kids constantly — use rider switch.
Ask for the back if you want the roughest ride; the front row has the best view of the light effects and a smoother run.
It gets an overlay for part of the year that changes the music, the effects, and the whole tone of the ride. If you want the standard version, check what is running before you queue.
Anything loose will go. There is no seat pocket, the ride is dark, and lost items are not retrievable until the end of the operating day.
The queue descends a long ramp and climbs back out. Factor that in for anyone with limited stamina, because it is longer than it looks from Tomorrowland.
attractions.bestTime: The first thirty minutes of the day, during the parade, or in the twenty minutes after the fireworks end.
attractions.typicalWait: 45 to 80 minutes for most of the day; 20 to 35 at open and close.

faqs.q: How tall do you have to be to ride Space Mountain at Disneyland?
faqs.a: 40 inches, the same as Big Thunder Mountain Railroad and Tiana's Bayou Adventure here. Note that Magic Kingdom's Space Mountain requires 44 inches, so a child who is too short in Florida may still clear it in California.

faqs.q: Is Space Mountain scary?
faqs.a: For a lot of people, yes, and darkness is the reason rather than the ride itself. There is no inversion and no significant drop, but you cannot see the track, so every turn and dip is a surprise. Children who love Big Thunder frequently refuse a second ride on this one.

faqs.q: How is Disneyland's Space Mountain different from Florida's?
faqs.a: Disneyland's has one track instead of two, seats riders two abreast instead of single file, runs a smoother and faster-feeling layout, and plays a synchronized soundtrack in each rocket. It also requires 40 inches rather than 44. Most people who have ridden both prefer the California version.

faqs.q: Can one adult ride with two small children?
faqs.a: No. One adult may supervise only one child under seven on Space Mountain, the same rule that applies to Matterhorn Bobsleds. If you are a single adult with two young riders, use rider switch — a cast member at the entrance will set it up.

faqs.q: Is there a big drop?
faqs.a: No. The drops are short and the top speed is moderate. What makes the ride intense is that you cannot see them coming. If your concern is a stomach-dropping plunge, Tiana's Bayou Adventure is the ride to worry about, not this one.

attractions.name: Star Tours: The Adventures Continue

scary.notes: A motion simulator with 3D glasses in a small cabin. Nothing frightening in the content, but the sensation of falling is convincing and the cabin pitches sharply. The bigger risk is nausea, not fear.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into a fixed seat with a seat belt in a cabin that pitches and rolls. Guests prone to motion sickness or with neck and back problems are advised against it. Captioning and audio description are available on request at the entrance.

attractions.summary: A motion simulator that randomizes its destinations, so no two rides are the same. 40 inches, and the queasiest ride in the park.
description: Star Tours opened at Disneyland in 1987 as Disney's first serious motion simulator and was rebuilt in 2011 as Star Tours: The Adventures Continue, swapping the single fixed storyline for a randomized structure. The ride selects an opening, a middle destination, a hologram message, and a finale from a pool of options, which means the specific five minutes you get is one of a very large number of combinations.

Sequels have added destinations over the years, so the pool keeps growing. Riding twice in a day and getting a completely different set of planets is the normal outcome, and it is the single best reason to ride it more than once.

It is also the most reliable nausea generator at Disneyland alongside Millennium Falcon. The cabin pitches on hydraulics while a 3D screen fills your field of vision, and there is no fixed horizon anywhere. People who never get motion sick get motion sick on this.
experience: The queue runs through a spaceport terminal with droids, luggage scanners, and departure boards, and it is genuinely funny in places if you read the signage. You collect 3D glasses, are seated in rows in a forty-passenger cabin, and belt in.

The ride starts with the shuttle taking off badly, then runs through the randomized sequence: a planetary destination with a chase or a crash, a hologram transmission, and a second destination with a set-piece finale. The screen work is sharp and the motion base is well synchronized to it, which is why the falling sensations land.

Sit in the middle rows if you are susceptible. The motion base amplifies at the extremes and the screen distortion is worst from the far edges. Take the glasses off if you start to feel unwell — it does not fix it entirely, but it helps more than closing your eyes.
tips: Ride it twice. The destinations are randomized and getting two different combinations is the normal outcome, not a lucky one.
If you get motion sick, middle rows and a fixed gaze on the center of the screen help. So does not riding it right after eating.
Disneyland's requirement is 40 inches, matching the Hollywood Studios version exactly.
The queue is air conditioned and one of the better places to wait in Tomorrowland on a hot day.
It is a decent Multi Pass use when the standby line is long, because unlike some rides here the wait genuinely does not drop much in the evening.
Someone in your row will be selected as the rebel spy and their face appears on screen. Sit toward the front if you want a chance at it.
attractions.bestTime: First hour of the day or during the parade. Waits stay fairly consistent otherwise.
attractions.typicalWait: 25 to 50 minutes. High capacity keeps it from getting truly out of hand.

faqs.q: How tall do you have to be to ride Star Tours?
faqs.a: 40 inches at Disneyland, the same as the version at Hollywood Studios. That is the same as Space Mountain, Big Thunder, Rise of the Resistance, and Millennium Falcon here, which makes 40 inches the number most worth knowing at Disneyland.

faqs.q: Is Star Tours the same ride every time?
faqs.a: No. Since the 2011 rebuild the ride randomizes its opening, destinations, hologram message, and finale from a growing pool of options. Two rides in a row will usually give you different planets and a different sequence, which is why locals ride it repeatedly.

faqs.q: Will Star Tours make me sick?
faqs.a: It is the most likely attraction at Disneyland to do so, along with Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run. The cabin moves on hydraulics while a 3D screen fills your vision with no fixed horizon. Middle rows help, as does riding on an empty-ish stomach.

faqs.q: Is it scary for children?
faqs.a: Not in content — there is nothing threatening in the way Indiana Jones or Rise of the Resistance are threatening. What bothers younger riders is the physical sensation of dropping and banking, and the volume. Most children over about six are fine.

attractions.name: Buzz Lightyear Astro Blasters

scary.notes: Dim black-light rooms full of cartoon targets, with a spinnable vehicle. Nothing frightening at any point, and the guest-controlled spin is optional.

accessibility.notes: Vehicles load from a slow-moving belt and there is a wheelchair-accessible car available on request at the entrance. The handheld blasters are on a cord and can be used from any seated position.

attractions.summary: A shooting-gallery dark ride where Disneyland's blasters come off the mount — a real advantage over the Florida version.
description: Astro Blasters opened at Disneyland in 2005 in the building that housed the old Circle-Vision theatre. You ride a two-person car through black-light rooms full of targets, scoring points by hitting them, with a joystick that spins the vehicle so you can aim at things behind you.

The key difference from Magic Kingdom's version is that Disneyland's blasters are handheld on a coiled cord rather than fixed to the car. You can aim them anywhere, hold them out the side, and hunt for the high-value targets that are impossible to hit from a fixed mount. It makes the scoring game considerably better.

Beyond that it is a modest ride with dated effects and a soundtrack that repeats. What keeps people coming back is the competition — the scores post at the end and families take it seriously enough that finding the high-value targets becomes the actual attraction.
tips: The blasters detach and are on a cord. Take yours out of the holster and aim freely — most first-timers never realize they can.
The highest-value targets are the small diamond and triangle shapes rather than the large obvious circles. The big glowing targets everyone shoots are worth the least.
Hold the trigger down rather than pulling repeatedly. The blaster fires continuously and the scoring registers on contact.
Use the joystick to spin backwards in the final room, where several high-value targets sit behind the vehicle.
It is on Multi Pass, but standby is usually reasonable and there are better uses of a selection in Tomorrowland.
attractions.bestTime: Any time. It has high capacity and the wait rarely becomes unmanageable.
attractions.typicalWait: 20 to 40 minutes. Moves steadily.

attractions.name: Finding Nemo Submarine Voyage

scary.notes: The submarine interior is narrow, enclosed, and windowless except for small portholes, which is a genuine problem for claustrophobic adults rather than for children. There is a dark sequence with an anglerfish and a shark that startles a few toddlers, and a section with rumbling volcanic effects.

accessibility.notes: Boarding requires descending a steep ladder-style stairway into the submarine hull, then sitting on a fixed stool facing a porthole for thirteen minutes. There is no wheelchair access to the submarines; an accessible alternative viewing experience is offered on the surface — ask at the entrance. This is the least accessible ride at Disneyland.

attractions.summary: Thirteen minutes inside a real submarine hull looking through portholes — claustrophobic, slow-loading, and unlike anything else.
description: The submarine lagoon dates to 1959 and is one of Disneyland's original engineering showpieces. The subs were retired in 1998 and the lagoon sat empty for nearly a decade before reopening in 2007 with a Finding Nemo story layered over the original hardware. The vessels are the same hulls, running the same submerged track around the same lagoon.

You descend into the hull, sit on a fixed stool facing a porthole, and watch a thirteen-minute underwater sequence combining physical sets in the lagoon with projections onto the water. Bubbles along the hull sell the illusion of diving even though the sub never actually submerges.

It is the most divisive attraction at Disneyland. The line is long, it moves badly because each sub holds few people and takes forever to load, the seats are hard, and the interior is genuinely tight. In exchange you get thirteen minutes of something no other theme park does, in a piece of 1959 infrastructure that should not still exist. Ride it once and decide for yourself; do not ride it on a one-day trip when the posted wait is over forty minutes.
experience: The queue runs along the lagoon in mostly open air with limited shade, which is the worst part of the whole thing on a summer afternoon. Boarding means going down a narrow stairway into the hull, single file, and then edging along a corridor to a stool.

Once seated, you are locked into one porthole for the duration with no ability to move. Your view is what your window shows and nothing else, which means the person opposite is watching a different ride. Portholes on the outer curve of the lagoon get the better scenes for most of the route.

The sequence runs through coral, a sunken structure, a dark trench with an anglerfish, a volcanic vent section with rumbling and heat, and a bright finale. The projection technology holds up better than it has any right to, and the moment the lights drop for the trench sequence is genuinely effective.
tips: If you are claustrophobic, do not ride. The hull is narrow, the stool is fixed, and thirteen minutes is a long time to discover you cannot leave.
The queue has poor shade and slow movement, which makes a 45-minute posted wait here far worse than a 45-minute wait almost anywhere else. Go in the first hour or the last.

Boarding is a steep, narrow stairway down into the hull. This is the least accessible attraction at Disneyland — there is a surface-level alternative for guests who cannot manage it, so ask at the entrance.
There is no height requirement, so babies can ride, but the sit-still-for-thirteen-minutes requirement is real for a toddler.
The submarine lagoon has been here since 1959 and the hulls are original. That context is most of why the ride is worth doing at all.
attractions.bestTime: The first hour of the day, or after dark when the queue is finally out of the sun.
attractions.typicalWait: 35 to 70 minutes and the line moves slowly. It is one of the worst wait-to-payoff ratios in the park at peak.

faqs.q: Is the Finding Nemo Submarine Voyage claustrophobic?
faqs.a: Yes, meaningfully so. You descend into a narrow steel hull, sit on a fixed stool facing a small porthole, and cannot move or leave for thirteen minutes. Adults who are uneasy in tight spaces should skip it, and there is no discreet way out once the sub is underway.

faqs.q: Does the submarine actually go underwater?
faqs.a: No. The subs ride a submerged track with their portholes below the waterline, and bubbles released along the hull sell the sensation of descending. You are looking through water at physical sets and projections in the lagoon, not diving.

faqs.q: Is there a height requirement?
faqs.a: No. Any age can ride, including infants. The practical limit is whether a small child will sit still on a fixed stool facing one window for thirteen minutes, which is a real question.

faqs.q: Can you ride in a wheelchair?
faqs.a: No. Boarding requires descending a steep, narrow stairway into the hull, which makes this the least accessible attraction in the park. Disneyland offers an alternative experience at surface level for guests who cannot board — ask a cast member at the entrance.

attractions.name: Astro Orbitor

scary.notes: Rockets that circle and tilt while you control your own height. It goes faster and higher than Dumbo and the angle at the top of the arc unsettles some children.

accessibility.notes: Rockets sit low with a high side and a cramped two-person seat that requires climbing over and folding down into. It is one of the more awkward transfers in the park for adults.

attractions.summary: Rockets that circle a bronze orrery at the Tomorrowland entrance — better than Dumbo, and a much worse queue.
description: Astro Orbitor sits at ground level at the entrance to Tomorrowland, unlike Magic Kingdom's version which is on the roof of the building. The rockets circle a spinning bronze armature of planets and rings, and each rider controls their own vehicle's height with a lever, tilting up to a steep angle at the top.

It is faster and higher than Dumbo and produces a genuine sensation, particularly from the outside seat as the rocket banks. The armature itself is beautiful — it is one of the few pieces of Tomorrowland that looks like the retro-future the land is supposed to be selling.

The problem is capacity and placement. Very few rockets, a ninety-second cycle, and a queue that sits in full sun on the main Tomorrowland walkway. A twenty-five-minute wait here in July is a poor decision, and a fifteen-minute wait in the evening is a good one.
tips: Ride it after dark. The armature is lit, the queue is out of the sun, and the whole thing is a completely different experience.
The rockets tilt steeply at full height. Keep the lever down if you are riding with a child who is nervous about heights.
It is one of the least capacity-efficient rides at Disneyland. If the posted wait is over 20 minutes, come back later.
The seat is cramped and requires stepping over a high side. Two adults will be uncomfortable; an adult and a child is the intended configuration.
attractions.bestTime: After dark, when the queue leaves the sun and the lighting is at its best.
attractions.typicalWait: 20 to 40 minutes for 90 seconds of ride — one of the worst ratios in the park.

attractions.name: Autopia
attractions.heightNote: 32in to ride with an adult; 54in to drive alone.

scary.notes: Driving a small car on a guide rail at walking-to-jogging pace. The engines are loud and the cars behind you will rear-end yours, which produces a jolt and a bang that startles some children. Nothing else about it is frightening.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into a low bucket seat in a small car, which is a difficult step down and up for guests with hip or knee limitations. The accelerator requires sustained foot pressure for five minutes, which is worth considering. Hand controls are not available.

attractions.summary: One of the last opening-day attractions still running, and the only place a six-year-old can drive. 32 inches to ride, 54 to drive alone.
description: Autopia has run since 1955 and is one of the few original opening-day attractions still operating in something like its original form. You drive a small car along a landscaped course with a center guide rail preventing you from leaving the track, at a speed somewhere between a brisk walk and a jog, for about five minutes.

The height numbers are the thing to know. A child needs 32 inches to ride with an adult and 54 inches to drive alone — and 54 inches is a big number, roughly a nine or ten-year-old. Parents routinely arrive assuming their seven-year-old will be driving solo and discover otherwise at the load platform.

The honest verdict is that it is loud, slow, smells of engine, and takes far longer to queue than it deserves. It also produces a specific, genuine thrill for a child holding a steering wheel for the first time, and there is nothing else at Disneyland that does that. Whether that trade is worth forty minutes depends entirely on who is in your party.
experience: The queue runs outdoors along the track with partial shade and moves slowly, because loading each car individually takes time. You are directed to a car, climb down into a low bucket seat, and take the wheel.

The driving itself is a matter of holding the accelerator and steering enough to keep the car from grinding along the guide rail — the rail does the real work, but a straight line still requires attention. The course runs past landscaping, under bridges, and alongside the second track, and the cars ahead and behind will bump you repeatedly.

Five minutes is longer than you think while holding an accelerator with a small foot. Adults riding with a small child usually end up working the pedal while the child steers, which is the standard arrangement and works fine.
tips: 54 inches to drive alone is the number that surprises people — it is a much taller requirement than the 32 inches to ride. Set expectations with your child before you get in line.
An adult can work the accelerator while a child steers. That is the normal arrangement for younger kids and cast members will not object.
Steer slightly toward the center of the lane rather than following the rail. Riding the rail is what produces the constant grinding and the jerky ride.
The queue is long, slow, and only partly shaded. If the posted wait is over 30 minutes, this is one of the weakest uses of that time in Tomorrowland.
It is on Multi Pass, and unusually, this is one of the better places to spend a selection precisely because standby is so inefficient.
Sit in the left car of a pair if you want the better view of the landscaping — the right lane runs closer to the fence.
attractions.bestTime: First hour of the day, or in the evening when the queue is out of the sun.
attractions.typicalWait: 30 to 60 minutes. Loading individual cars keeps the line slow no matter the crowd level.

faqs.q: How tall do you have to be to drive at Autopia?
faqs.a: 32 inches to ride as a passenger with an adult, and 54 inches to drive alone. That 54-inch figure is a lot taller than most parents expect — it typically means a child of about nine or ten. Younger children ride with an adult who usually works the pedal.

faqs.q: Can my child steer if they are not tall enough to drive alone?
faqs.a: Yes. The standard arrangement for younger children is that the adult operates the accelerator while the child holds the wheel. Cast members see this all day and will not stop you, and it is by far the most satisfying version of the ride for a five-year-old.

faqs.q: Is Autopia worth the wait?
faqs.a: Only if you have a child who wants to drive. It is loud, slow, and consistently posts one of the least efficient waits in the park. With a six-year-old holding a steering wheel for the first time it is one of the best things in Disneyland; without one, skip it.

faqs.q: How long is the ride?
faqs.a: About five minutes of driving, which is longer than most guests expect and long enough that a small child's leg will get tired holding the accelerator. That is the main reason adults end up working the pedal.

attractions.name: Disneyland Monorail
attractions.closedNote: Closed for refurbishment since March 30, 2026. Disney has not announced a reopening date. Walk between Tomorrowland and Downtown Disney in the meantime; the walk from the Tomorrowland station area to the Downtown Disney station is roughly 10 to 15 minutes.

scary.notes: An elevated train running a fixed beam at moderate speed. Nothing frightening; the height of the beam is the only thing anyone reacts to.

accessibility.notes: When operating, the monorail is boarded via a ramp at platform level and accommodates wheelchairs and ECVs without transfer, though the doors and aisles are narrow. Stations are reached by ramp or elevator.

attractions.summary: The 1959 monorail between Tomorrowland and Downtown Disney, closed for refurbishment since March 30, 2026.
description: The Disneyland Monorail opened in 1959 as the first daily-operating monorail in the Western Hemisphere and runs a loop from a station in Tomorrowland out over the Disneyland Hotel area to a station in Downtown Disney, and back. A full round trip takes roughly thirteen minutes, and it is one of the few attractions that doubles as genuine transport — you can exit at Downtown Disney and re-enter the park later with a valid ticket.

It has been closed for refurbishment since March 30, 2026, and Disney has not announced a reopening date. Plan on walking between Tomorrowland and Downtown Disney; the walk takes roughly ten to fifteen minutes and passes the park's main entrance.

It is listed here because it is a frequently searched attraction and because the Downtown Disney station is a genuinely useful exit route on a busy evening when the main gate is congested. When it returns, that exit is worth remembering.
tips: It is not operating. Budget a 10 to 15 minute walk between Tomorrowland and Downtown Disney instead.
When it does operate, the Downtown Disney station is a far calmer way to leave the park at closing time than the main gate.
The front cabin behind the driver has the best view and cast members allocate it on request at the station — worth asking for when it returns.
Do not build a day plan around it reopening. No date has been announced.
attractions.bestTime: Not operating.
attractions.typicalWait: Not operating.
